Distinguish present-day topography from historical sheets, satellite imagery and cadastral boundaries. |
| **P08 Census, statistics and time series — C19** | [Census developer geography guidance](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/geography.html), official statistical agencies and state/local statistical bureaus | OGD India, MoSPI, Census of India, RBI statistics and state statistical abstracts as source families | Topic/indicator + geography + period → dataset/table/series ID, unit, denominator, geography code and reference period. Housing-tenure statistics are aggregate information, not a register of individual owners. |
| **P09 Environmental and public infrastructure data — C19** | Federal/state environmental, water and transport agencies; public utilities' published datasets; local open-data catalogs | Pollution-control boards, water/public-works departments, transport authorities and state/city open-data catalogs | Facility/station/route/area + variable/time → public observation, inventory, permit or infrastructure dataset. Distinguish measured observations, modeled values and proposed infrastructure. |

## Find sources systematically, jurisdiction by jurisdiction

Build two jurisdiction trees before gathering hundreds of URLs. For the USA use
federal → state/territory → county/equivalent → municipality, recording tribal
government catalogs where appropriate. Start from [USAGov state links](https://www.usa.gov/state-governments)
and its local directory, then verify the actual agency responsible for the record.
Use official geography identifiers where supplied; the [Census API geography
documentation](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/geography.html) illustrates
why a county code without its state is ambiguous.

For India use Union → state/UT → district → subdistrict/tehsil → municipality or
village/panchayat. The [India district web directory](https://www.india.gov.in/directory/web-directory/districts)
and [Local Government Directory dataset](https://data.gov.in/catalog/local-government-directory-lgd)
are starting points. Follow official revenue, registration, planning, statistical
and geological offices from there. Record renamed/split districts and the vintage
of boundary codes; a village name alone is not a stable record identity.

For each of C08/C18/C19, expand an initial pool toward roughly 50–75 US and
50–75 India candidate origins, then replenish from observed pass rates. Sample
across geography, language, urban/rural context and government level. To approach
100 qualified sources, broaden jurisdictions and responsible agencies rather
than counting 100 datasets from one city as 100 sources. National aggregators
can cover several attributed origins, but membership and coverage require proof.

Research queries vary by record type:

```text
P01: site:{agency-domain} (publications OR reports) "{topic}" "{year}"
P02: site:{legislature-or-gazette-domain} "{act/rule title}" "{jurisdiction}"
P03: site:{city-domain} (minutes OR resolutions OR budget OR awards) "{year}"
P04: "{county/state}" (recorder OR assessor OR land records) (API OR open data)
P05: site:{planning-domain} (permits OR zoning OR master plan) (catalog OR GIS)
P06: "{state}" "geological survey" (map catalog OR GIS OR publications)
P07: site:{mapping-agency-domain} "{place/sheet}" (topographic OR land cover)
P08: site:{statistics-domain} "{indicator}" "{district/county}" (table OR API)
P09: site:{agency-domain} "{water/transport/environment theme}" (data OR services)
```

Use native-script/local terms for India, including भूलेख, खसरा, खतौनी, பட்டா and
சிட்டா where relevant. Keep the official terminology and script in results;
transliteration is a discovery aid, not authority to join two records. Search
engine hits identify candidates; they do not establish access or record contents.

## From a directory entry to something the app can query

Investigate these routes in order, and record the actual supported capabilities:

1. **Official document/dataset catalog API.** [GovInfo documents an API search
   service](https://www.govinfo.gov/features/search-service-overview) for content
   and metadata. The current [Data.gov Catalog API](https://resources.data.gov/catalog-api/)
   searches dataset metadata and identifies publisher organizations; it explicitly
   replaces the previous CKAN API. Use the current interface and key policy,
   not an old tutorial. An indexed dataset still needs a valid resource link.
2. **Approved exports and local metadata search.** Small DCAT/CSV/JSON/XML catalogs
   can become bounded, reviewed search artifacts without a hosted database. Prefer
   metadata and canonical outbound links; do not copy whole national parcel or
   imagery stores to make a prototype searchable.
3. **Native record or feature queries.** A source can qualify for property or
   spatial lookup through real address/parcel/document-ID/area queries even when
   it lacks general keyword search. This must return record metadata and a usable
   destination; an identifier-shaped redirect to an external search page is not
   retrieval. Record this as a separate capability from topic discovery.
4. **Geo services with explicit discovery.** [OGC WFS](https://www.ogc.org/standards/wfs/),
   [OGC API Features](https://www.ogc.org/standards/ogcapi-features/) and documented
   [ArcGIS layer queries](https://developers.arcgis.com/rest/services-reference/enterprise/query-feature-service-layer/)
   are patterns to inspect for spatial/attribute filtering. Confirm the deployed
   service's capabilities, limits, IDs and terms; the platform brand is not proof.
   [WMS](https://www.ogc.org/standards/wms/)/WMTS primarily deliver rendered maps
   or tiles. A searchable layer catalog can support map discovery, but does not
   establish searchable parcel attributes or downloadable source features.

Track three separate capabilities: **find a dataset/map/document**, **query
records within it**, and **read/view/download the result**. A catalog hit for
property data cannot answer “which record covers this parcel?” unless the second
capability is present. Conversely a spatial result can be useful without hosting
a map renderer: a precise official map/document link is a valid initial action.

Maintain one selected live connector per request and bounded local searches.
Route by explicit country/jurisdiction, record type and supported query mode;
do not fan out to every county or district. The register records unsearched
coverage. A failed jurisdiction query does not establish absence of the record.

## Property and maps: two concrete pilot cases

**USA property:** NYC's official ACRIS page documents searchable property records
and document images for four boroughs, and also states bandwidth/automation
restrictions. Investigate the separately published [ACRIS Master dataset](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/ACRIS-Real-Property-Master/bnx9-e6tj)
and its native data dictionary as a metadata route; prove document/parcel joins,
current terms and canonical image links before qualification. Do not extrapolate
its geographic coverage to all New York City or all US counties. This is one
illustrative local case, not a model every recorder must support.

**India property:** Tamil Nadu's official land e-services page lists rural
Patta/Chitta/FMB and urban TSLR resources and describes free FMS copies. It also
warns that automatic translation can change names in Tamil extracts. These facts
make it a strong discovery lead; they do not demonstrate an authorized external
API. Check supported metadata/record interfaces, the actual free access path,
survey/subdivision identifiers and allowed automation before enabling it. Service
or certification fees are distinct from freely viewing an informational record.

For both, preserve issuer, jurisdiction, record type and “as of” date. Assessment
roll ownership, recorded transaction parties, records of rights and registered
title serve different purposes. Return the official source's classification and
published redactions; do not silently infer current ownership from an older deed
or build unrelated personal profiles by joining records across authorities.

For maps, store native map/layer/sheet ID, source URL, geographic extent, coordinate
reference system, axis order, scale/resolution, legend, survey/observation date,
publication/update date and data lineage where provided. A geology map at regional
scale must not appear to be a precise parcel survey. Survey date and download
date are separate; historic maps remain historical even when newly digitized.

## First batch and acceptance tests

Allocate **six US and six India origins within the overall 60-origin deep-review
cap**, deduplicating any shared candidates. This is not an additional 12 reviews.
For each country select one reports/law route, one civic-budget route, one
property route, one permits/planning route, one geological/topographic route and
one statistics/environment route. Within a broad national catalog, inspect the
origin-specific attribution; include state/local cases rather than selecting
only national aggregators. NYC and Tamil Nadu are initial local case studies.

Before the next batch, complete the [source review template](../SOURCE_REVIEW_TEMPLATE.md)
and these track-specific checks using provider examples or public institutional
locations where possible:

- **Reports/law/civics:** retrieve a known document by title and number, separate
  amendments and editions, recover a dated meeting/decision and prove fiscal-year
  filtering. Confirm the canonical complete document rather than its announcement.
- **Property/planning:** test native parcel/address/document lookup in the correct
  jurisdiction; ambiguous address and nonexistent parcel; leading zeros; parcel
  splits/renumbering; mismatched assessment versus deed dates; permit status versus
  approved plan. Display unavailable/unknown when the requested join is unsupported.
- **Geology/maps:** retrieve a known sheet by ID and bounding box; test an extent
  crossing administrative boundaries; verify longitude/latitude order and CRS;
  distinguish map layer, legend and feature response. Check scale/date constraints,
  no-coverage responses and source-service limits without stress-testing the host.
- **Statistics/environment:** test geography code plus period, units, denominator,
  missing/suppressed values and boundary-vintage changes. Never convert a missing
  observation into zero or present an aggregate estimate as a household fact.
- **All tracks:** prove usable free access, paging/export bounds, permission,
  current source attribution and at least two representative sessions. Fixture-test
  failures and quotas. Free registration is acceptable; CAPTCHA, paid document
  access or restricted APIs may require deferral, never circumvention.

Report progress by country, government level, P-track and capability. For each
of C08/C18/C19 pursue the 10 → 25 → 50 → 100 qualified-origin ladder using measured
conversion and geographic gaps. Separately report origins enabled in the product;
one source's 5,000 layers does not replace the 100-origin goal.

## Evidence status and next verification

This was documentation research, not an API qualification run. Current official
Data.gov, GovInfo, USGS TNM, Census, USAGov, NYC and Tamil Nadu pages were readable;
their documentation supports the proposed discovery routes, not an availability
guarantee. Data.gov's current migration notice is especially important for future
connector selection. Keys, terms, quota settings and actual result samples still
need checking before implementation.

Direct opens of data.gov.in timed out, DILRMP's older state-link page and NGDRS
state links returned 502 in the research tool, NGMDB returned 403, and the older
Bhuvan WMS wiki URL returned 404 despite remaining in search results. Bhuvan's
homepage exposed only a loading shell; NGDR terms could not be opened. Official
search results identified GSI/NGDR and land-directory leads, but no machine-query
or free post-login behavior is certified. Record these gaps and recheck the
operator's current documentation; do not interpret the tool failures as national
service outages or a reason to invent an endpoint.

# Scholarly research discovery playbook

Planning research, 2026-11-05. Covers C03 published articles, C06 theses and
dissertations, and C07 preprints/working papers. Apply the counting and admission
rules in [the expansion plan](../EXPANSION_PLAN.md) and record each investigation
with [the source template](../SOURCE_REVIEW_TEMPLATE.md). These are documented
research routes; no new origin has been qualified or enabled by this review.

## C03 — Published research articles

**Start with publisher and repository discovery, then prove individual holdings.**
[OpenDOAR](https://opendoar.ac.uk/help/about) supplies institutional repository
leads. [SciELO](https://www.scielo.org/en/) supplies country, publisher and subject
entry points, particularly useful for Latin American and regional-language
coverage. DOAJ remains a directory lead; the current direct DOAJ connector
deferral is unchanged. Separate the publisher, journal collection, repository
copy and index that found it.

| Research track | Where to look and how to expand |
| --- | --- |
| International | Follow SciELO's publisher lists and country nodes; use OpenDOAR to identify university/research repositories; inspect disciplinary society publishers. Rotate medicine, engineering, agriculture, social sciences and humanities instead of taking the first 100 biomedical origins. |
| USA | Start with university repository catalogs and official learned-society publication lists. Separate institution-hosted open manuscripts from subscription publisher versions. Federal research agencies can also supply journal-article deposits; an agency bibliography alone is insufficient. |
| India | Use [INFLIBNET's initiatives](https://www.inflibnet.ac.in/activities/) and [university directory](https://web.inflibnet.ac.in/universitydirectory/index.php) to locate official institution sites. Follow their repository and society-publisher links, sampling central/state universities and research institutes. ONOS/N-LIST institutional entitlements are not evidence of anonymous public access. |

Repeatable discovery searches:

```text
site:{official-university-domain} (repository OR "open access") "{discipline}"
"{society name}" journals (metadata OR OAI-PMH OR API)
"{Indian institution}" (शोध OR ஆய்வு OR research) repository
```

Resolve organization names to stable identities before counting. The first
research batch is ten independent origins: four Indian, four broadly accessible
international and two additional regional-language origins. Deep-review one
publisher and one repository with the greatest apparent coverage gap. Expand in
25-origin batches across countries, disciplines and organization types toward
100 qualified origins; journal titles from one catalog do not become 100 origins.

**Retrieval strategy.** Test existing OpenAlex coverage first, using a known work
and its actual host attribution. Current [OpenAlex search documentation](https://help.openalex.org/api/searching/)
describes work text/keyword search and separate entity searches; an institution
name match does not establish that its repository holds the paper. Use the
documented filters and inspect individual locations. Preserve the existing free
allowance guard. A new publisher API or permitted OAI/export import is justified
when the index demonstrably misses useful holdings. An OJS website or a DOI
registration record alone does not prove reusable full-item discovery.

**Category-specific proof.** Use five known articles spanning recent/older years,
at least two subjects and relevant local-language content. Confirm topic relevance
with agriculture, manufacturing or another industry topic, not just exact titles.
Resolve DOI/native ID to the same article and test its free destination. Include
a hybrid-journal paywalled article, accepted manuscript versus published version,
retraction/correction and missing full-text location where present. Keep valid
versions distinct; a source-wide OA label cannot make every location free.

## C06 — Theses and dissertations

**Start from degree-granting institutions and national thesis networks.**
[NDLTD's FAQ](https://ndltd.org/thesis-resources/faqs/) describes a union catalog
made available to service providers and directs users to its current Find ETDs
resources; its navigation currently points Global ETD Search to OATD. Treat this
as a directory/coverage route, not evidence of a turnkey NDLTD keyword API.
Cross-reference university origins through OpenDOAR.

| Research track | Where to look and how to expand |
| --- | --- |
| International | Follow NDLTD's member/resource links to national thesis services and their contributing universities. Sample different languages and degree systems; a national portal is an index unless it hosts the authoritative deposit. |
| USA | Inspect official university library ETD policies and institutional repositories. Check whether the institution supplies open deposits or only points to a commercial dissertation service. University departments are not extra origins when their theses share one maintained catalog. |
| India | Begin with Shodhganga through [INFLIBNET's official initiatives](https://www.inflibnet.ac.in/activities/), then follow university links. Use the official university directory's state/category browsing to fill geographic gaps. [IndCat's documented features](https://indcat.inflibnet.ac.in/index.php/main/features) include thesis discovery and Shodhganga links, but a bibliographic record is not itself a readable thesis. |

Search recipes:

```text
site:{university-domain} ("electronic theses" OR dissertation OR thesis) repository
"{university name}" (OAI-PMH OR "metadata harvesting")
"{state or university}" (शोधप्रबंध OR ஆய்வேடு) repository
```

The first ten candidates should include four Indian university origins from
different states, two US universities and four institutions in other regions.
Select two deep reviews with different repository platforms/languages. Build the
next batches from uncovered degree institutions, not repeated national-portal
collections. Five discovery regions with 20 qualified institution catalogs each
is a research allocation toward 100, subject to actual conversion and overlap.

**Retrieval strategy.** Verify attributed aggregator coverage with known thesis
titles first. Otherwise inspect the repository's advertised OAI-PMH/export or
documented API. OAI-PMH requires an import and local title/topic search; it is not
a live keyword endpoint. Discover actual supported routes and versions instead
of guessing DSpace paths. Start with a bounded, disclosed metadata subset using
the existing catalog approach; no new hosted database is prerequisite.

**Category-specific proof.** Check complete dissertation versus abstract/synopsis,
degree, university, award year, native handle and content language. Sample a
multi-file/chapter thesis, embargoed deposit, scanned document and duplicate
national/institutional copy. Search Hindi/Tamil titles in native script where
claimed; compare transliteration separately. Successful retrieval of a title page
or one chapter does not establish access to the whole thesis. Document OCR/full-text
limitations, withdrawn records and how embargo changes will be refreshed.

## C07 — Preprints and working papers

**Use two different discovery paths: disciplinary servers and institutional series.**
[ASAPbio's server directory](https://asapbio.org/preprint-servers/) describes
server scope and practices. [RePEc's archive directory](https://ideas.repec.org/archives.html)
identifies institutional archive providers, but explicitly says its listing is
not current. Follow its archive templates and each institution's current site;
do not derive today's coverage totals from that list.

| Research track | Where to look and how to expand |
| --- | --- |
| International | Use ASAPbio for disciplinary server leads, SciELO's preprint link for regional coverage, and RePEc archive/provider links for economics and social-science working-paper collections. Sample more than one discipline. |
| USA | Follow university/research-center working-paper series and government research-unit publications from their official sites. Record whether a series is independently maintained or part of the institution's existing repository origin. |
| India | Follow Indian institutions in RePEc and the INFLIBNET university directory; inspect economics, management, engineering and agricultural research repositories. Include native-language series where actually present; an English institutional website does not prove English-only holdings. |

Search recipes:

```text
site:{institution-domain} ("working papers" OR "discussion papers" OR preprints)
"{series name}" (ReDIF OR metadata OR repository OR API)
"{discipline}" "{country}" "preprint server"
```

For the first ten origins, investigate four Indian institution collections, three
international disciplinary servers and three institutional series from other
regions, including the USA. Deep-review one server and one working-paper archive.
To approach 100, replenish both paths in batches of 25 and deduplicate operators.
There may not be 100 suitable independent preprint servers; institutional
working-paper catalogs supply a distinct, valid part of this category. One
university's many series still count as one catalog origin under the main rules.

**Retrieval strategy.** Prefer existing attributed aggregator search where its
coverage passes. The [bioRxiv/medRxiv API documentation](https://api.biorxiv.org/)
supports date-window/DOI metadata retrieval and version information; it is not a
generic keyword search interface. A permitted bounded metadata import can make
that feed searchable locally. [RePEc's metadata policy](https://ideas.repec.org/getdata.html)
prefers publisher archives/ReDIF over website scraping and requires prior contact
for commercial use. Review applicability before use; no outreach is sent as part
of this plan. Direct arXiv automation remains deferred under the current plan.

**Category-specific proof.** Search five known preprints/working papers, including
an older version, updated version, published successor, withdrawn item and a
paper without DOI where those cases exist. Preserve native handle, series/number,
version date and exact reading destination. Publication relations are links,
not a reason to merge distinct versions. Test topic results for industry terms
and label preprints clearly; being publicly readable is not peer-review evidence.

## Handoff and research limits

Each ten-candidate batch produces the origin register, two completed qualification
records, a category benchmark, unsupported-query notes and the next directory
expansion. Report aggregate overlap across C03/C06/C07 before estimating work.
Scale only after measuring pass rates and useful new coverage.

This review inspected official directory/protocol documentation, not production
API behavior, source-login access or complete catalogs. The old OpenAlex docs URL
failed after redirect; the linked Help Center route worked. RePEc's root page
returned a gateway error while its archive/policy pages worked. These are tooling
observations, not evidence of source-wide downtime. Current prices, permission,
freshness and per-origin free access still require qualification before enablement.

# Source catalog and connection options

Research date: 2026-10-31. Update 2026-11-01: [additional probes and Book Dash delivery](ADDITIONAL_SOURCES.md). Reconstructed for MyBookshelf-web; see [provenance](README.md#repository-transfer-and-evidence-provenance) and [historical API observations](evidence.json). Provider rules and quotas need rechecking before enabling a connector.

**Roles:** host supplies the reading destination; index describes items hosted elsewhere; resolver finds a location from an identifier. Some providers perform several roles.

**Effort:** low = documented search and straightforward mapping; medium = imports, XML, edition/access reconciliation or account setup; high = feed agreement or unresolved public integration. These are relative integration estimates, not delivery promises.

**Priority:** P0 = initial implementation; P1 = subsequent coverage; P2 = investigate or arrange access. No public API verified means this research did not establish one, not that none exists.

## 1. General ebooks and public-domain literature

| Source / role | How the app can search it | Reading destination and access distinction | Credentials, constraints, effort / priority |

No generic HTML scraper is needed for the first release. Search-engine scraping, subscription bypasses and unauthorized shadow libraries are excluded. Build a **metadata discovery service with outbound reading links**. Use a hybrid of locally indexed metadata catalogs and a small number of live search adapters. The app should not download or serve the books or papers themselves.

This is feasible with free sources. The difficult parts are deciding whether a specific edition is actually readable, keeping source permissions and quotas current, and combining overlapping records without losing versions or translations. Free content does not imply an unlimited free search API.

## Recommendation

Start with **Free books** and **Research papers**. Add **Textbooks & learning** through the Open Textbook Library catalog, then a curated **Children's books** collection. Treat language, subject, reading level, format, and access conditions as separate filters rather than mutually exclusive categories.

| Open Textbook Library | Official CSV/JSON metadata; local search | Documented CC0 catalog for educational material |
| DOAJ | Live article search | OA journal articles with publisher full-text links |
| Europe PMC | Live search and record details | Biomedical literature with explicit full-text/OA fields |
| arXiv | Atom API behind a shared request queue | Direct preprint coverage with clearly labeled versions |
| OpenAlex | Live search after key/budget verification | Broad multidisciplinary discovery and OA locations; usage is metered |
| DOAB / OAPEN | Metadata imports and OAI-PMH updates | Scholarly books and chapters; next import candidates |

Reuse Google Books and Open Library selectively to enrich book records and resolve existing saved books to candidate free editions. Their general catalogs contain previews, borrowing offers, and metadata-only records; they should not define the free-reading collection by themselves.

## What the original checks established

Structured responses were obtained from Google Books (using the configured key), Open Library, Internet Archive, DOAJ, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, Europe PMC, CORE, Zenodo, HAL, Wikisource, Library of Congress, and LibriVox. Gutenberg RDF and DOAB record/harvesting responses also worked. OAPEN's OAI service identification worked; a record import was not exercised.

These were small one-time checks, not integration, rights, uptime, completeness, or user-country tests. Important counterexamples:

- An Open Library work returned `ebook_access: public` alongside many Internet Archive identifiers. That does not identify which edition is freely readable.
- A HAL hit had a record URL and DOI but no `fileMain_s`: a repository hit is not necessarily full text.
- Zenodo returned a dataset; item-type filtering is essential.
- DOAJ supplied an older HTTP publisher URL; metadata alone does not prove the destination still works.
- Semantic Scholar returned **429**, and Gutendex timed out. Those checks do not establish general service availability.
- Some documentation URLs moved; corrected DOAB/OAPEN URLs appear in the catalog. Some sites returned only a JavaScript shell. NCERT/ERIC/OER Commons could not be fully inspected.

Two current details make older integration advice unreliable: Standard Ebooks' full OPDS feeds require membership/access arrangements, and Unpaywall's documentation said its title-search endpoint retired on **2026-09-18**. Use Unpaywall for DOI resolution and another index for search. Recheck these policies before implementation.

## Credentials and implementation inputs

No additional credentials are needed to review this plan. The original Google Books free-ebook query succeeded using the configured key. For implementation:

1. Verify **`OPENALEX_API_KEY`** in the backend. The replacement environment reports the variable configured; no authenticated OpenAlex request was made during this repository transfer. At the research date the free account included $1/day of API usage, roughly 1,000 ordinary search requests before caching. Disable paid overages unless deliberately budgeted.
2. Choose a real **application contact email** for request identification and, if enabled, Unpaywall's required `email` parameter. No email was invented, registered, or sent during this work.
3. Optional later: Semantic Scholar, BHL and Europeana keys; CORE upgrade/eligibility confirmation. Standard Ebooks feed access and children's/OER catalog feeds need provider-specific arrangements.

Assumptions: global discovery with explicit language/country context; lawful public hosts; verified free source login is allowed (owner clarification 2026-11-01), labelled separately from anonymous reading; no full-text hosting, subscription purchases, or library-card integration. Existing India library coverage makes NCERT, DIKSHA, StoryWeaver and Shodhganga useful follow-ups, but their discovery integrations are not assumed ready.

source status, partial/unavailable/empty/limit/loading states, the children's
pilot and a desktop layout. Records on the boards are samples.

Owner decisions on the proposal:

1. Keep the four app tabs. Free to read and Papers are scopes inside Search.
2. Free books and papers can be saved to the shelf. Storage for items without
   ISBNs still needs an engineering design before implementation.

7. A free book links back to the reader's library by title search, without
   treating the two as the same edition.

# Search across connected knowledge sources

Owner authorization, 2026-11-05: release the researched search integrations to
production and let users search across data sources. This implementation is on
`feat/free-knowledge-search`, in its own worktree from current production main.
The separate recurring research task remains research-only; its unfinished
registry and candidate counts are not production qualification.

## Behavior

The new **All knowledge** search submits one query to connected providers with
at most three requests in flight. Results arrive independently and remain grouped
by source; an outage, empty page or limit at one provider cannot erase another's
results. Source, type and supported language filters are visible before searching.
Each group has independent continuation and retry. Native identities, editions,
recordings, source credits, rights and free-account labels are preserved. A user
can open a canonical result, read/listen on the original site and save it using
the existing browser shelf behavior. Library search and the existing Free to read
and Papers views remain available.

Ten new integrations are released behind `CONTENT_KNOWLEDGE_ENABLED=true`:
Global Digital Library, LibriVox, Library of Congress digital books, Biodiversity
Heritage Library's Internet Archive collection, African Minds, LSE Press,
Mattering Press, mediastudies.press, punctum books and Python 3.15 documentation.
Five publisher catalogs share Thoth; this is not five separate API infrastructures.
The existing Gutenberg, Open Textbook Library, Book Dash and StoryWeaver snapshots
and the existing OpenAlex/Europe PMC integrations are also selectable. With the
existing production flags, this gives 16 connected sources, not 16 fully audited
origins or complete catalogs.

Wikipedia, Wikibooks and Wikisource remain disconnected: the current robots
policies disallow the reviewed `/w/api.php` search route. No alternate route was
used to evade this restriction. arXiv/DOAJ retain their existing pacing-related
exclusion from live requests. Other registry candidates require supported query,
access or credential work before integration. This release does not make an
unverified directory or research lead searchable by merely listing it.

## Contracts and limits

- One provider per server request; the browser coordinates the search. No Redis,
  SQL, hosted cache, persisted session or new account/service.
- Fixed-origin adapters bound response size, deadline and paging. Signed cursors
  bind provider, query, types, language, page size and expiry; they work across
  function restarts without storing query results. Changed indexes can change
  pages; exact-key deduplication never merges similar titles or distinct editions.
- The new transport serializes requests per host within an instance, spaces them
  two seconds apart and honors 429 Retry-After. It has no automatic retries.
  This courtesy is not a global request quota across Vercel instances.
- Python's official compressed symbol inventory is bounded and cached for one
  hour in process memory. Search is over symbol/section names, not arbitrary
  full documentation text. Version and same-origin URL checks fail closed.
- GDL uses its public content-search route and published WordPress REST book-ID
  route for exact details. Word-level metadata checks reject substring noise
  such as `Rain` matching only `Shakrain`. Its provider offset advances even when
  inspected rows fail relevance, so filtering does not trap pagination.
- Thoth searches active monographs/edited books in explicit publisher IDs. Exact
  resolution verifies publisher membership and active status. Only canonical
  digital links on reviewed publisher hosts become reading/download actions;
  print, retail and unreviewed mirrors do not.
- LoC requires `access_restricted=false`, digitization and an online resource for
  free access. BHL searches only its biodiversity collection and excludes known
  access-restricted items. Their content rights still vary by item.
- LibriVox is title search and distinct recording identity. Its documented JSON
  404 for no audiobooks is an empty result; other errors remain failures. US
  public-domain statements do not claim worldwide rights.
- Snapshot sources remain labelled incomplete/stale when appropriate. Unknown
  access is hidden by default; an explicit checkbox reveals labelled results with a source record link; no old
  observation is refreshed merely because a user searches it.
- Existing OpenAlex free-allowance and zero-paid-balance checks remain unchanged.
  No key is returned to the browser. No full books/audio are copied.

## Verification and release record

Current live results, including source IDs and reading links, are in
[evidence/knowledge-release-2026-11-05](evidence/knowledge-release-2026-11-05/).

subsequent search, detail and paging passed. These are retained as failures, not
relabelled successes. Test failures caused by local socket permission were rerun
with loopback networking enabled; no application security setting was weakened.

Final build, test counts, hosted deployment and production verification are

Median (EMA72)

Median
The median of a data set is the value in the central position, when the data set has been arranged from the lowest to the highest value.

Note that exactly half of the values from the data set are less than the median and the other half are greater than the median.

To calculate the median of a quantitative data set, first sort the data from the smallest to the largest value and then find the value in the middle. If there is an odd number of values in the data set, the median will be equal to one of the values in the data set. If there is an even number of values in the data set, the median will lie halfway between two values in the data set.

WORKED EXAMPLE 4: MEDIAN FOR AN ODD NUMBER OF VALUES

What is the median of {10;14;86;2;68;99;1}?

Sort the values
The values in the data set, arranged from the smallest to the largest, are

1;2;10;14;68;86;99
Find the number in the middle
There are 7 values in the data set. Since there are an odd number of values, the median will be equal to the value in the middle, namely, in the fourth position. Therefore the median of the data set is 14.

WORKED EXAMPLE 5: MEDIAN FOR AN EVEN NUMBER OF VALUES

What is the median of {11;10;14;86;2;68;99;1}?

Sort the values
The values in the data set, arranged from the smallest to the largest, are

1;2;10;11;14;68;86;99
Find the number in the middle
There are 8 values in the data set. Since there are an even number of values, the median will be halfway between the two values in the middle, namely, between the fourth and fifth positions. The value in the fourth position is 11 and the value in the fifth position is 14. The median lies halfway between these two values and is therefore

Mode (EMA73)

Mode
The mode of a data set is the value that occurs most often in the set. The mode can also be described as the most frequent or most common value in the data set.

To calculate the mode, we simply count the number of times that each value appears in the data set and then find the value that appears most often.

A data set can have more than one mode if there is more than one value with the highest count. For example, both 2 and 3 are modes in the data set {1;2;2;3;3}. If all points in a data set occur with equal frequency, it is equally accurate to describe the data set as having many modes or no mode.

The following video explains how to calculate the mean, median and mode of a data set.

Video: 2GM5

From the table above we can see that 4 is the only value that appears 3 times. All the other values appear less than 3 times. Therefore the mode of the data set is 4.

One problem with using the mode as a measure of central tendency is that we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set. Since continuous values can lie anywhere on the real line, any particular value will almost never repeat. This means that the frequency of each value in the data set will be 1 and that there will be no mode. We will look at one way of addressing this problem in the section on grouping data.

I. Background
We periodically issue regulations
requiring changes in the labeling of
food. If the compliance dates of these
labeling changes were not coordinated,
the cumulative economic impact on the
food industry of having to respond
separately to each change would be
substantial. Therefore, we periodically
have announced uniform compliance
dates for new food labeling
requirements (see, e.g., the Federal
Register of October 19, 1984 (49 FR
41019); December 24, 1996 (61 FR
67710); December 27, 1996 (61 FR
68145); December 23, 1998 (63 FR
71015); November 20, 2000 (65 FR
69666); December 31, 2002 (67 FR
79851); December 21, 2006 (71 FR
76599); December 8, 2008 (73 FR
74349); December 15, 2010 (75 FR
78155); November 28, 2012 (77 FR
70885); December 10, 2014 (79 FR
73201); November 25, 2016 (81 FR
85156); December 20, 2018 (83 FR
65294); January 6, 2021 (86 FR 462); and
January 3, 2023 (88 FR 6)). Use of a
uniform compliance date provides for
an orderly and economical industry
adjustment to new labeling
requirements by allowing sufficient lead
time to plan for the use of existing label
inventories and the development of new
labeling materials.
II. Analysis of Environmental Impact
We have determined under 21 CFR
25.30(k) that this action is of a type that
does not individually or cumulatively
have a significant effect on the human
environment. Therefore, neither an
environmental assessment nor an
environmental impact statement is
required.
III. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995
This final action contains no
collections of information. Therefore,
clearance by the Office of Management
and Budget under the Paperwork
Reduction Act of 1995 is not required.
IV. Conclusion
This action does not relate to existing
requirements for compliance dates
contained in final rules published
before January 1, 2025. Therefore, the
compliance dates for all final rules
published by FDA in the Federal
Register before January 1, 2025, will be
the date stated in the respective final
rule. We generally encourage industry to
comply with new labeling regulations as
quickly as feasible, however. Thus,
when industry members voluntarily
change their labels, it is appropriate that
they incorporate any new requirements
that have been published as final
regulations up to that time.

ACTION: Final action. SUMMARY: FSIS is establishing January 1, 2028, as the uniform compliance date for new meat and poultry product labeling regulations that will be issued between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2026. FSIS periodically announces uniform compliance dates for new meat and poultry product labeling regulations to minimize the economic impact of label changes. DATES: Effective date: This action is effective November 27, 2024. Compliance date: The uniform compliance date for new meat and poultry product labeling regulations that will be issued between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2026, is January 1, 2028. Comments due date: Comments on this final action must be received on or before December 27, 2024. ADDRESSES: FSIS invites interested persons to submit comments on this rule. Comments may be submitted by one of the following methods: Federal eRulemaking Portal: This website provides the ability to type short comments directly into the comment field on this web page or attach a file for lengthier comments. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Background On December 14, 2004, FSIS issued a final rule establishing January 1, 2008, as the uniform compliance date for new meat and poultry labeling regulations issued between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2006 (69 FR 74405). The 2004 final rule also provided that the Agency would set uniform compliance dates for new labeling regulations in 2-year increments and periodically issue final rules announcing and requesting comments on those dates. Consistent with the 2004 final rule, the Agency has since published nine rules establishing the uniform compliance dates of January 1, 2010, January 1, 2012, January 1, 2014, January 1, 2016, January 1, 2018, January 1, 2020, January 1, 2022, January 1, 2024, and January 1, 2026 (72 FR 9651, 73 FR 75564, 75 FR 71344, 77 FR 76824, 79 FR 71007, 81 FR 91670, 83 FR 63052, 85 FR 81339, and 87 FR 77707). The Final Rule The new uniform compliance date will apply only to final FSIS regulations that require changes in the labeling of meat and poultry products and that are published after January 1, 2025, and before December 31, 2026. For each final rule that requires changes in labeling, FSIS will specifically identify January 1, 2028, as the compliance date. All meat and poultry food products that are subject to labeling regulations issued between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2026, will be required to comply with these regulations on products introduced into commerce on or after January 1, 2028. If any food labeling regulation involves special circumstances that justify a compliance date other than January 1, 2028, the Agency will determine an appropriate compliance date and will publish that compliance date in the rulemaking. Two-year increments increase industry's ability to make orderly adjustments to new labeling requirements without exposing consumers to outdated labels. This approach allows meat and poultry producers to plan for the use of label inventories and to develop new labeling materials that meet the new requirements. It also serves to reduce the economic impact of changing labels on both producers and consumers. In the March 5, 2007, final rule, FSIS received only four comments on the announced uniform compliance dates, all in support. In the March 5, 2007, final rule, FSIS determined that further rulemaking for uniform compliance dates for labeling requirements is unnecessary (72 FR 9651). The Agency received no comments on the 2007 final rule, the comments FSIS received on the 2012 final rule were outside the scope (77 FR 76824), and FSIS received no comments on the 2014 final rule (79 FR 71007) or the 2016 final rule (81 FR 91670). The Agency received four comments on the 2018 final rule (83 FR 63052), all in support. The Agency received four comments on the 2020 final rule (85 FR 81339); one was outside the scope of the rulemaking and three were in support of the rule. The Agency received two comments on the 2022 final rule (87 FR 77707); one was in support of the rule, and one requested a 90-day extension because of potential supply chain issues for self-adhesive label materials. Because the commenter did not provide any additional information to support their claim about supply shortages and no other members of industry expressed concerns about a shortage, FSIS did not change the uniform compliance date. Consistent with its statement in 2007, FSIS finds that further rulemaking on this matter is unnecessary. However, FSIS is providing an opportunity for comment on the uniform compliance date established in this final rule. { "schema_version": 1, "observed_at": "2026-11-05 11:43:52 UTC", "repository": "fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api", "provider": "GitHub connector", "scope": "Public provider documentation; repository CC0 code license is not automatically a blanket license for every hosted spending-data field.", "files": [ { "path": "README.md", "content": "#

[![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![Pull Request Checks](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api/actions/workflows/pull-request-checks.yaml/badge.svg?branch=staging)](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api/actions/workflows/pull-request-checks.yaml) _This API is utilized by USAspending.gov to obtain all federal spending data which is open source and provided to the public as part of the DATA Act._ ![USAspending Landing Page](readme.jpg?raw=true "Readme") ## Creating a Development Environment Ensure the following dependencies are installed and working prior to continuing: ### Requirements - [`docker`](https://docs.docker.com/install/) which will handle the other application dependencies. - [`docker compose`](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) - `bash` or another Unix Shell equivalent - Bash is available on Windows as [Windows Subsystem for Linux](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install-win10) - [`git`](https://git-scm.com/downloads) - [`make`](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/) for running build/test/run targets in the `Makefile`. (Run `$ make` for a list of targets.) _**If not using Docker, you'll need to install app components on your machine:**_ > _Using Docker is recommended since it provides a clean environment. Setting up your own local environment requires some technical abilities and experience with modern software tools._ - Command line package manager - Windows' WSL bash uses `apt` - MacOS users can use [`Homebrew`](https://brew.sh/) - Linux users already know their package manager (`yum`, `apt`, `pacman`, etc.) - [`PostgreSQL`](https://www.postgresql.org/download/) version 16.x (with a dedicated `data_store_api` database) - [`OpenSearch`](https://www.elastic.co/downloads/elasticsearch) version 2.9 - `Python` version 3.12 environment - Highly recommended to use a virtual environment. There are various tools and associated instructions depending on preferences - See [Required Python Libraries](#required-python-libraries) for an example using `uv` - [`uv`](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) python package/project manager ### Cloning the Repository Now, navigate to the base file directory where you will store the USAspending repositories ```shell mkdir -p usaspending && cd usaspending git clone https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/usaspending-api.git cd usaspending-api ``` ### Environment Variables Choose an option between `.env` and `.envrc` that best fits your preferred workflow. Pay close attention to the values in these environment variables as usage of `localhost` vs a container's name differ between local setups. #### Create Your `.env` File (recommended) Copy the template `.env` file with local runtime environment variables defined. Change as needed for your environment. _This file is git-ignored and will not be committed by git if changed._ ```shell cp .env.template .env ``` A `.env` file is a common way to manage environment variables in a declarative file. Certain tools, like `docker compose`, will read and honor these variables. #### Create Your `.envrc` File _[direnv](https://direnv.net/) is a shell extension that automatically runs shell commands in a `.envrc` file (commonly env var `export` commands) when entering or exiting a folder with that file_ Create a `.envrc` file in the repo root, which will be ignored by git. Change credentials and ports as-needed for your local dev environment. ```shell export DATABASE_URL=postgres://usaspending:usaspender@localhost:5432/data_store_api export ES_HOSTNAME=http://localhost:9200 export BROKER_DB=postgres://usaspending:usaspender@localhost:5432/data_broker ``` If `direnv` does not pick this up after saving the file, type ```shell direnv allow ``` _Alternatively, you could skip using `direnv` and just export these variables in your shell environment._ **Just make sure your env vars declared in the shell and in `.env` match for a consistent experience inside and outside of Docker** ### Build the Docker Images _:bangbang: Re-run these commands if any python package dependencies change (in `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock`), since they are baked into the docker image at build-time._ #### usaspending-backend | usaspending-download _These images are used as the basis for running the API and download containerized setup services._ ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending build ``` #### usaspending-development _This image is used as the basis for local development including but not limited to: tests, spark jobs, linting, etc._ ```shell docker compose --profile test build ``` ### Database Setup A postgres database is required to run the app. You can run it in a `postgres` docker container (preferred), or run a PostgreSQL server on your local machine. In either case, it will be empty until data is loaded. - :warning: If running your own PostgreSQL server be sure to: 1. Have a DB named `data_store_api` 2. A superuser role (user), e.g. `ALTER ROLE <> WITH SUPERUSER;` 3. Cross-check your `.env` or `.envrc` files if used to be sure it references your DBs user, password, host, and port where needed ##### Start the Postgres DB Container _If not using your own local install..._ ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-db ``` ... will create and run a Postgres database. Use the following commands to create necessary users and set the `usaspending` user's search_path ```shell docker exec -it usaspending-db sh -c " \ psql \ -h localhost \ -p 5432 \ -U usaspending \ -d data_store_api \ -c 'CREATE USER etl_user;' \ -c 'CREATE USER readonly;' \ -c 'ALTER USER usaspending SET search_path TO public,raw,int,temp,rpt;' \ " ``` ##### Bring DB Schema Up-to-Date - To run [Django migrations](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/2.2/topics/migrations/). ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py migrate ``` - To provision the materialized views which are required by certain API endpoints. ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py matview_runner --dependencies ``` ##### Seeding and Loading Database Data _To just get essential reference data, you can run:_ - To load essential reference data (agencies, program activity codes, CFDA program data, country codes, and others). ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage python3 -u manage.py load_reference_data ``` _Alternatively, to download a fully populated production snapshot of the database (full or a subset) and restore it into PostgreSQL, use the `pg_restore` tool as described here: [USAspending Database Download](https://onevoicecrm.my.site.com/usaspending/s/database-download)_ - Recreate matviews with the command documented in the previous section if this is done _**Executing individual data-loaders** to load in data is also possible, but requires more familiarity with those ad-hoc scripts and commands, and also requires an external data source (Data Broker DB, or external file, etc.) from which to load the data._ - For details on loading reference data, Data Accountability Broker Submissions, and current USAspending data into the API, see [loading_data.md](loading_data.md). - For details on how our data loaders modify incoming data, see [data_reformatting.md](data_reformatting.md). ### OpenSearch Setup Some API endpoints reach into OpenSearch for data. ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-es ``` ... will create and start a single-node OpenSearch cluster as a docker container with data persisted to a docker volume. - The cluster should be reachable via at http://localhost:9200 ("You Know, for Search"). - Optionally, to see log output, use `docker compose logs usaspending-es` (these logs are stored by docker even if you don't use this). While not required, it is highly recommended to also create the OpenSearch Dashboards docker container for querying the OpenSearch cluster. ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up -d usaspending-kibana-es ``` #### Generate Elasticsearch Indexes The following will generate the indexes: ```shell CURR_DATE=$(date '+%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S') docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-transactions" --load-type transaction docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-awards" --load-type award docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-recipients" --load-type recipient docker compose run --rm usaspending-manage elasticsearch_indexer --create-new-index --index-name "$CURR_DATE-subaward" --load-type subaward ``` ### Observability/Tracing Setup The project uses grafana, tempo, and opentelemetry for observability. This enables developers to trace functionality across multiple services resulting in better visibility of issues. There are two options for using the observability framework in the local development setup. You can log traces to the console by setting the `TOGGLE_OTEL_CONSOLE_LOGGING` environmental variable to `True` for the `usaspending-api` container. Alternatively you can run the `otel-collector`, `tempo`, and `grafana` containers to more fully replicate the production observability framework. These containers are part of the `tracing` profile and can be brought up with: ```shell docker compose --profile tracing up -d ``` When using these containers the `TOGGLE_OTEL_CONSOLE_LOGGING` must be set to `False` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` must be set to `http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces` ### Install python version with uv Install the currently supported python version with uv. This is useful for access to a python shell outside a container. However, it is recommended to use the docker compose containerized services for interaction with the API, spark, and tests. ```shell uv python install 3.12.11 ``` #### Sync uv project with lockfile Setup uv project and check version info: ```shell make local-dev-setup ``` ## Running the API Run the following to bring up the Django app for the RESTful API: ```shell docker compose --profile usaspending up usaspending-api ``` You can update environment variables in `settings.py` (buckets, elasticsearch, local paths) and they will be mounted and used when you run this. The application will now be available at `http://localhost:8000`. _**NOTE**: if the code was run outside of Docker then compiled Python files will potentially trip up the docker environment. A useful command to run for clearing out the files on your host is:_ ```shell find . | grep -E "(__pycache__|\.pyc|\.pyo$)" | xargs rm -rf ``` #### Using the API In your local development environment, available API endpoints may be found at `http://localhost:8000/docs/endpoints`. Deployed production API endpoints and docs are found by following links here: `https://api.usaspending.gov`. ## Running Tests ### Test Setup 1. Build the base `usaspending-development` Docker image (the test container is based on this Docker image). In the parent **usaspending-api** directory run: ```shell docker build -t usaspending-development -f development.Dockerfile . ``` 2. Start the Spark containers for the Spark related tests ```shell docker compose --profile spark up -d ``` 3. To run all USAspending tests in the docker services run ```shell docker compose run --rm -e BROKER_DB='' usaspending-test ``` _**NOTE**: If an env var named `BROKER_DB` is set, Broker Integration tests will attempt to be run as well. If doing so, Broker dependencies must be met (see below) or ALL tests will fail hard. Running the above command with `-e BROKER_DB=''` is a precaution to keep them excluded, unless you really want them (see below if so)._ To run tests locally and not in the docker services, you need: 1. **Postgres**: A running PostgreSQL database server _(See [Database Setup above](#database-setup))_ 1. **OpenSearch**: A running OpenSearch cluster _(See [OpenSearch Setup above](#opensearch-setup))_ 1. **Environment Variables**: Tell python where to connect to the various data stores _(See [Environment Variables](#environment-variables))_ 1. **Install python version with uv**: python is installed with uv _(See below)_ 1. **Sync uv project**: uv project is synced with lockfile _(See below)_ _**NOTE**: Running test locally might require you to run `export OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY=YES`. As discussed [here](https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/38560), there is an issue than can cause some of the Spark tests to fail without this environment variable set._ ### Including Broker Integration Tests Some automated integration tests run against a [Broker](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency/data-act-broker-backend) database. If certain dependencies to run such integration tests are not satisfied, those tests will bail out and be marked as _Skipped_. (You can see messages about those skipped tests by adding the `-rs` flag to pytest, like: `pytest -rs`) To satisfy these dependencies and include execution of these tests, do the following: 1. Ensure the `Broker` source code is checked out alongside this repo at `../data-act-broker-backend` 1. Ensure you have [`Docker`](https://docs.docker.com/install/) installed and running on your machine 1. Ensure you have built the `Broker` backend Docker image by running: ```shell docker build -t dataact-broker-backend ../data-act-broker-backend ``` 1. Ensure you have the `BROKER_DB` environment variable set, and it points to what will be a live PostgreSQL server (no database required) at the time tests are run. 1. _WARNING: If this is set at all, then ALL above dependencies must be met or ALL tests will fail (Django will try this connection on ALL tests' run)_ 1. This DB could be one you always have running in a local Postgres instance, or one you spin up in a Docker container just before tests are run 1. If invoking `pytest` within a docker container (e.g. using the `usaspending-test` container), you _must_ mount the host's docker socket. This is declared already in the `docker-compose.yml` file services, but would be done manually with: `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` _**NOTE**: Broker source code should be re-fetched and image rebuilt to ensure latest integration is tested_ Re-running the test suite using `pytest -rs` with these dependencies satisfied should yield no more skips of the broker integration tests. **Example Test Invocations of _Just a Few_ Broker Integration Tests:** (_i.e. using `-k`_) _From within a container_ _**NOTE**: `BROKER_DB` is set in the `docker-compose.yml` file (and could pick up `.env` values, if set)_ ```shell docker compose run --rm usaspending-test pytest --capture=no --verbose --tb=auto --no-cov --log-cli-level=INFO -k test_broker_integration ``` _From Developer Desktop_ _**NOTE**: `BROKER_DB` is set in the `.envrc` file and available in the shell_ ```shell pytest --capture=no --verbose --tb=auto --no-cov --log-cli-level=INFO -k test_broker_integration ``` ## Contributing To submit fixes or enhancements, or to suggest changes, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Conventional irrigation systems, such as channel irrigation and wild flooding tend to waste water as large quantities are supplied to the field in one go, most of which just flows over the crop and runs away without being taken up by the plants.

Micro irrigation is an approach to irrigation that keeps the water demand to a minimum. It has been driven by commercial farmers in arid regions of the United States of America and Israel in farming areas where water is scarce.

Typically, these commercial irrigation systems consist of a surface or buried pipe distribution network using emitters supplying water directly to the soil at regular intervals along the pipework. They can be permanent or portable.

Many parts of the world are now using micro irrigation technology. The systems used by large commercial companies are generally quite complex with an emphasis on reducing the amount of labour involved.

Small-scale farmers in developing countries have been reluctant to take up micro irrigation methods due to the initial investment required for the equipment. A number of organizations have looked at ways to simplify and reduce the cost of micro irrigation resulting in the approaches of drip irrigation and pipe irrigation. For these small-scale irrigation systems not only should the technical aspects of the system be considered such as:

access to reliable water sources
a secure and well-fenced garden
basic gardening skills
the crops grown
The social aspects should also be of concern to ensure the irrigation system will be of benefit. The social and economical factors will include:

capital and financial management; credit facilities
the availability of external services
maintenance
market opportunities for the produce
willingness to show other farmers the technology
Drip irrigationeditedit source
Drip irrigation uses low-cost plastic pipes laid on the ground to irrigate vegetables, field crops and orchards. This technology was developed in the 1960s for commercial use. Circa 1990 a US firm called Chapin Watermatics developed a low-cost system called bucket kits, which use standard plastic buckets and lengths of hose that could be cut to the appropriate lengths.

Small holes in the hose allow water to drip out and keep the base of the plant wet without wasting any water. The kits are low-cost, easy to assemble and manage. They do not need high quality water, providing the water is filtered. A 20 litre bucket with 30 metres (100 feet) of hose or drip tape connected to the bottom. The bucket is placed at least 1 metre (3 feet) above the ground so that gravity provides sufficient water pressure to ensure even watering for the entire crop. Water is poured into the bucket twice daily and passes through a filter, fills the drip tape and is evenly distributed to 100 watering points. The multi-chambered plastic drip tape is engineered to dispense water through openings spaced at 30cm (12 inches).


Figure 2: Jane Kirambia and Practical Action farmers project staff examine the drip irrigation kit. Tharaka Farmers' Project, Kenya (copyleft Practical Action /Morris Keyonzo)
Two bucket kits costing around $20 will produce enough vegetables for a family of seven and can last over five years. The system is most suited to kitchen gardens. As well as the bucket, you will need several strong poles, tools, manure, water and vegetable seedlings. The poles are used to make a support structure for the bucket. The stand should hold the bucket about 1 metre above the ground. The main stages of setting up the systems are:

a hole should be cut carefully into the base of the bucket
the hole is fitted with the filter plug and tubing and then flushed out to ensure that the system is clean.
the drip lines are then connected and the system is flushed out again before the ends of the drip lines are closed off.
The whole procedure of setting up the system will only take about one hour, including the construction of the bucket support. When planting a seedling is planted at each wet spot so that all the moisture is absorbed directly by the plant roots. Moving the kit from plot to plot tends not to be very practical and damages the equipment. It is better to add extra buckets and lines when necessary or when funds are available to invest in additional equipment.

The advantages are:

the effort to water the plants is greatly reduced
the time taken to fill the containers is significantly less than manually watering the planted area.
the growth of weeds is reduced as water does not reach unwanted plants.
Some initial training is required to show how to get the best results from the system and careful attention should be taken to a number of common problems that occur with the system comprising of:

clogging of the trip tapes especially if water is not well filtered. The emitters can be cleaned by blowing dirt out and then flushing out the particles with clean water.
leakage at connections: this can be checked and corrected
weeding must avoid puncturing the tape
vermin can damage pipes in their search for water
theft of equipment
The bucket kit is the smallest type of drip irrigation available. Although productivity is increased providing greater food security and improved nutrition, the amount of water and labour saved is small. Often there is not sufficient surplus produce for users to sell and provide financial benefits.

Bigger containers can be used to suit larger market gardens. Large customised drum kits irrigating a high-value crop offer greatest financial impact.

A research project on Affordable Micro Irrigation Technology (AMIT) was conducted by Intermediate Technology Consultants (ITC) and International Development Enterprises (IDE) in India and Zimbabwe. The looked at the constraints to adoption of low-cost, improved, drip irrigation technologies by poor farmers. The findings are available on ITC's website.

In East Africa drip irrigation has been promoted by Practical Action East Africa and the Arid Land Information Network (ALIN) who sell drip irrigation kits similar to the ones used in India and Zimbabwe.


Figure 3: Water is poured into the pipe which then irrigates the plants at the roots (copyleft Barbara Bryant/Practical Action)
Pipe irrigationeditedit source
The use of buried clay pitchers is an ancient technique of subsurface irrigation. The use of clay pipes had been initially tried in Russia and Mexico. ITDG Southern Africa along with others in Zimbabwe developed a low cost variation of this irrigation method in which clay pipes were buried beneath vegetable beds of the 450 women members of garden groups.

One end of the pipe is blocked and the other is tilted out of the soil to allow filling. The pipes were laid end to end below the soil surface. When the pipe is filled, water will gradually escape from the cracks between the pipe sections and through the pores in the clay to provide a continuous supply of water to the vegetables.

The objective of this project is to create a solar cooker out of local invasive species and waste materials. We want to create a device that can pasteurize water and be an alternative to the use of fossil fuels for cooking food. Our criteria for evaluating the appropriateness of technology are: use of local materials, efficiency, durability, ease of use, ease of construction, cost, impact on environment, impact on culture/lifestyle, education or expertise needed for construction.

Overall this was a successful project. We were able to meet our goal of pasteurizing water. The solar basket can pasteurize water in a quart container in about an hour with optimal conditions. If we were to make the solar basket version 2.0, here are some changes we would make:

Double up the blackberry runners so that the ribs of the basket are stronger
Use another material instead of pampas grass because it causes lumps on the basket's surface, maybe something softer
Use all large can lids, of the shiniest quality
Construct the rings that hold the parabolic shape out of a less flexible material than the aluminum and wire that we found
Project Coordinator: Bart Orlando

Student Engineers: Ginger Fletcher-Santillan and Ana Kolpin

General Research on Parabolic Solar Cookerseditedit source
Parabolic solar cookers are devices for preparing food that do not require fuel. They concentrate the sun's rays to one focal point where a dark pot or pan can be used to cook with. There are many advantages and disadvantages to using a solar cooker. Some of the advantages are: they can be used in places where there is little available fuel, they do not pollute, the outside of the parabolic shape does not get hot, they can be made out of recycled and local materials and they do not cost anything to operate. Some disadvantages are: the area to cook on is only big enough for one pot, cooking can only be done on sunny days, cooking time can take longer than when using a conventional stove or oven, the cooker may need to be refocused as the sun shifts. (Working Group on Development Techniques 1990)

Since parabolic solar cookers do not require fuel, they are being experimented with in many developing countries around the world as an alternative and supplement to cooking with fire. In India, a study was conducted to assess the utility of parabolic solar cookers in household use. The criteria for the assessment included ease of operation, initial cost, need for training, aesthetics, and overall safety. The overall conclusion of the study was that the parabolic solar cooker has a pretty high utility but in order for them to be commercialized, "The utility on technical, behavioral and commercial aspects should be improved." (Pohekar, Ramachandran 2006).

According to the Solar Cooker Review, a man in Vietnam has started producing solar cookers made out of local baskets. The cookers consist of a basin surrounded by insulation set in a basket made of local materials. The solar cookers are well suited to the central and northern provinces of Vietnam which receive 2-3000 hours of sunlight a year (Solar Cooker Review 2000).

Parabolas and Paraboloidseditedit source
The three dimensional parabola, the paraboloid, is the most efficient shape for solar cookers. Unlike box solar ovens, the parabolic shape has a central focal point where any light that hits the parabola's walls will reflect into it. Using sunlight, the heat, along with the light, will reflect into that focal point and warm that spot. The cooking container should be located at the focal point so the maximum amount of heat will be used for cooking.

Himalaya Blackberryeditedit source
The structure of the parabolic solar cooker will be made from the canes, or stems, of the locally invasive Himalaya blackberry. Canes will be harvested and dethorned so they can be woven into a parabolic basket shape.

The Himalaya blackberry, Rubus procerus, is an evergreen that was brought to the United States from Europe in the early nineties (Everett, 1981). It has a vigorous trailing growth pattern and it is heavily thorned. Since the canes will be harvested during the winter months, they will be dried, sturdier, and easier to dethorn and manage. The Himalaya blackberry canes form parabolic curves, so when they dry and stiffen they will maintain the sturdy parabolic shape of the basket (Figure 1).

Although blackberries cannot withstand extreme climates and grow mostly during the springtime (Whatcom), the Himalaya has a rapid growth rate of around 20 to 50 feet per season (Bailey, 1961) causing it to spread and takeover areas. The Himalaya blackberry is an invasive, non-native species to Humboldt County, and California state government has provided funding for the removal of the species throughout regional and state parks (California Department of Parks and Recreation, 2005) so harvesting them for the basket will not have a negative environmental impact on the area.

Humboldt County Weathereditedit source
The amount of clear days in Humboldt County is the major inconvenience with local solar cooking. Eureka has around 78 completely clear days per year with the most during September and October and a monthly average of 6.5 clear days (Western Regional Climate Center). Although most days are not completely clear, there are still partly cloudy days where it will clear up long enough to cook something around midday to early afternoon.
